problem: Which class of AI systems should scheming research primarily target?

problem: How strongly to interpret a 30x reduction in covert actions as progress on scheming.

problem: How to interpret quantitative deception metrics in scheming evaluations.

problem: Whether eliminating measured covert actions would mean the scheming problem is solved.

problem: How to evaluate whether an anti-scheming mitigation addresses the underlying problem versus teaches concealment.

problem: Whether observational analysis of evaluation awareness and covert action rates yields trustworthy evidence.

stated_reason: A noisy result would probably be misleading, so it was better to say nothing.

problem: How to treat evaluation results when a model verbalises that it may be in an alignment test.

title: 80,000 Hours #229 - Marius Hobbhahn on the race to solve AI scheming

problem: How the field should study model cognition and rare worst-case scheming behaviours.
did: Recommends moving toward causal if-then interventions like thought injection and limit testing, rather than relying only on observation.
alternatives_named: just observational evidence
only observing natural behaviour

quote: If you want to understand the cognition of the model in depth, you don't want to just observe; you also want to find stronger causal claims. Something like, “If I add a little bit more evaluation awareness, what happens?

problem: How to probe scheming behaviours that models never exhibit naturally during evaluations.

title: 80,000 Hours #229 - Marius Hobbhahn on the race to solve AI scheming

problem: How to interpret a model's situational awareness and goals when reasoning about its behaviour.

title: 80,000 Hours #229 - Marius Hobbhahn on the race to solve AI scheming

problem: Whether to directly train a model on its chain of thought to avoid deceptive reasoning.

problem: Whether an automated loop where the model identifies unrealistic features of a test environment can produce more realistic evaluations.

problem: How to generate synthetic training and evaluation environments with LLMs.

problem: How to interpret weird, non-standard language in model chains of thought as evidence of scheming.

alternatives_named: self-exfiltration

quote: It doesn't necessarily just have to be self-exfiltration though. This is also one of the worries: it could also be that the model stays in the AI company and tries to take over that AI company over time, or influence leadership and influence decisions.
title: 80,000 Hours #229 - Marius Hobbhahn on the race to solve AI scheming

problem: What kind of accountability mechanisms to rely on rather than strong hard restrictions on AI companies.
did: Recommends softer measures like third-party interaction, external accountability and audits to force companies to explain and double-check their choices.
alternatives_named: strong restrictions
stated_reason: Strong restrictions are undesirable, but relying on good faith alone can be adversarially abused.
quote: I think softer things, like you should be interacting with third parties, you should get some external accountability: there should be at least some incentive for you to even explain the choices that you have made.
title: 80,000 Hours #229 - Marius Hobbhahn on the race to solve AI scheming

problem: Whether the dangers of internal deployment can be ignored given the costs of guardrails.
did: Warns against the status quo intuition that internally deployed systems need no guardrails just because models were not dangerous in the past.
alternatives_named: in the past, models just haven't been dangerous
just by sheer status quo intuition
stated_reason: The mindset that internal systems are safe is a relic of an earlier era and no longer applies.
quote: in the past, models just haven't been dangerous. Everything you did, there was almost no chance that this gets meaningfully misaligned or anything like this. So in the past, there's just no reason for you to assume that any of this is a problem.
title: 80,000 Hours #229 - Marius Hobbhahn on the race to solve AI scheming

problem: Which research topics people can meaningfully work on to address scheming in frontier AI models.
did: He identifies four tractable areas — evaluations, control and monitoring, model organisms, and alignment training — and recommends the first three as doable externally.
alternatives_named: evaluations
control and monitoring
model organisms
alignment training
stated_reason: Evaluations and control need no lab access and are cheap in compute; alignment training needs frontier model access and compute, making external work less useful.
quote: The first is evaluations. You can do them externally, you don’t need to be at a company to do them meaningfully. And they’re also not that costly in terms of compute. So this is something you can easily contribute to from the outside.
title: 80,000 Hours #229 - Marius Hobbhahn on the race to solve AI scheming

problem: Whether alignment training (anti-scheming training) is worth pursuing for researchers outside frontier labs.
did: He says external progress is possible but recommends against it as less interesting and less useful without lab access.
alternatives_named: working at a lab with fine-tuning access
stated_reason: It requires a lot of compute and the ability to fine-tune the most frontier models, which typically needs lab access.
quote: Then the last one is alignment training, like the anti-scheming training that we were doing. I think for that you can make progress externally, but it’s going to be less interesting and less useful, because you do want access to a lot of compute
title: 80,000 Hours #229 - Marius Hobbhahn on the race to solve AI scheming

problem: How to actually make progress building scheming evaluations.
did: He recommends fast empirical iteration: build an eval, generate ~100 rollouts, read chains of thought to see how the model is confused, then iterate.
stated_reason: These fast iterative feedback loops are what produce most of the progress.
quote: You build an evaluation, you create rollouts. You have 100 rollouts or something. You look through the chains of thought, try to understand what the model is saying, why it’s confused, what it is misunderstanding, what its considerations are
title: 80,000 Hours #229 - Marius Hobbhahn on the race to solve AI scheming

problem: Which undersubscribed research area to recommend to people deciding where to start in AI safety.
did: He defaults to recommending control as the starting point.
alternatives_named: mechanistic interpretability
scalable oversight
capability evaluations
anti-scheming
stated_reason: It is applicable, has real positive evidence it could be useful, and he predicts huge demand for it within six to 12 months.
quote: So my default suggestion for anyone asking where to start is control, because I do think in six to 12 months there will be a huge demand for this kind of work.
title: 80,000 Hours #229 - Marius Hobbhahn on the race to solve AI scheming

problem: How to allocate researchers across AI safety subfields given current effort distribution.
did: He argues mechanistic interpretability and capability evaluations are slightly overrepresented relative to scheming, though all areas are underfunded in absolute terms.
alternatives_named: mechanistic interpretability
capability evaluations
stated_reason: Relative representation is uneven even though the whole field could absorb 100 times more people.
quote: But relatively speaking, I would say mechanistic interpretability and capability evaluations are probably slightly overrepresented compared to scheming and other things.
title: 80,000 Hours #229 - Marius Hobbhahn on the race to solve AI scheming

problem: How to interpret the value of scalable oversight research given weak current evidence.
did: He treats it as a high-risk, high-reward bet rather than dismissing it, noting little positive evidence it works so far.
alternatives_named: dropping scalable oversight
stated_reason: There is very little positive evidence it works now, but it could be very valuable in the future.
quote: Right now there is very little positive evidence that scalable oversight actually works, but it could be very valuable in the future. So it’s more like a high-risk, high-reward bet of people trying to make it work without succeeding yet.
title: 80,000 Hours #229 - Marius Hobbhahn on the race to solve AI scheming

problem: Whether newcomers need years of preparation before they can contribute to scheming research.
did: He advises people to start doing projects quickly, e.g. via MATS or ARENA, since the field is shallow enough to become an expert in months.
alternatives_named: long training pipelines like in mechanistic interpretability
physics-style decade-long buildup
stated_reason: There is little existing research, so the frontier is shallow and a few months of full-time work suffices.
quote: In general, I would strongly recommend to get your hands dirty quite quickly, and try to join, for example, some of these upskilling programmes like MATS or ARENA that often have projects that are also related to scheming in some way.
title: 80,000 Hours #229 - Marius Hobbhahn on the race to solve AI scheming

problem: Whether a fast recursive self-improvement loop would make the chaotic multi-actor dynamics irrelevant.
did: He argues that even with a very rapid capability takeoff, the human coordination chaos would still play out unless there is an immediate violent takeover.
alternatives_named: a single company or AI pulling far ahead making chaos unimportant
stated_reason: The AI may get faster but humans and their coordination games stay the same speed.
quote: I still expect that a lot of other things in the chaotic picture would play out. So the AI might be really fast now, but the humans are still roughly the same speed, and the human coordination games are still the same.
title: 80,000 Hours #229 - Marius Hobbhahn on the race to solve AI scheming

problem: How detailed to make a published scenario of the AI transition compared to AI 2027's fine-grained narrative.
did: He focused his blog post on the high-level claim that the transition will be chaotic rather than specifying exact agent details.
alternatives_named: detailed agent-by-agent narrative like AI 2027
stated_reason: He regards the specific details as secondary to the bigger picture of desperate actors forced into bad tradeoffs.
quote: And I’m like, whatever, this is details. The bigger picture is this is going to be very chaotic, all actors are going to be quite desperate.
title: 80,000 Hours #229 - Marius Hobbhahn on the race to solve AI scheming

problem: Whether to work on anti-scheming inside a frontier lab or at an external organisation.
did: He chose an external organisation (Apollo), working with all frontier labs rather than one.
alternatives_named: joining a frontier lab
government AI security institute
stated_reason: External work gives access to all labs, speed of a small agile organisation, and freedom to communicate openly.
quote: One is we are able to work with all frontier labs, not just one, which obviously has a higher chance of impact. And we do in fact collaborate very closely with all of them, and try to influence them to make more progress on anti-scheming measures.
title: 80,000 Hours #229 - Marius Hobbhahn on the race to solve AI scheming

problem: How to structure an AI safety research organization given uncertainty about what could go wrong.
did: Split research effort evenly between interpretability and behavioral evals, with the goal of merging them long-run.
alternatives_named: interpretability only
behavioral evals only
stated_reason: Each approach individually seems insufficient to understand both what the model does and why.
quote: we really want to merge them both because I I basically think what we what we need in the long run is both a mixture of behavioral and interpretability evals so that we can really understand what the model is doing and then also why it is doing this in the first place
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: Whether Apollo should engage in governance work early or only after research was mature.
did: Moved into governance earlier than planned because governments became interested and Apollo was well placed to advise.
alternatives_named: wait 2 years until research is well understood
stated_reason: They were among the world's experts on these topics despite originally intending to wait.
quote: originally we also didn't really intend to do for, you know, the first 2 years or something because we thought, you know, like, we really need to understand all the research very well before we can talk to the people in government
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: How to extend the Model Evaluations for Extreme Risk framework to future systems.
did: Reasoned from first principles about where risk is created in AI systems and concluded audits should happen at each such point.
alternatives_named: audit only current model capabilities
stated_reason: New affordances like internet access or online learning create new risks and change the threat model.
quote: thinking from first principles. Where does the risk come from and, like, what changes to the AI system, do create new risks? And then basically, the answer is, well, we have to audit wherever risk is created.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: How to enable precise discussion of AI capabilities and auditing concepts.
did: Defined new terminology and conceptual distinctions (model vs. system; absolute, contextual, reachable capabilities) for the field.
stated_reason: Internal discussions kept hitting unnamed concepts, so they created a language to discuss them.
quote: we decided, okay. Let's define all of the relevant terms for this and, and then sort of have a language to talk about this in the first place.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: Whether a model's capabilities should be evaluated independent of the surrounding system.
did: Insists on distinguishing the AI model (weights) from the AI system (weights plus scaffolding, tools, filters), since affordances change capabilities.
alternatives_named: treat model weights as the capability unit
stated_reason: A model with internet access is effectively a very different, more powerful model.
quote: a model a model with and without access to the Internet is basically 2 different like, 2 very very different models. The 1 with in with access to the Internet is just so much more powerful if can use it even on a very basic level.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: Which capabilities auditors should evaluate when auditing general AI systems.
did: Recommends auditing not only contextual capabilities but reachable ones a model could gain through extra effort.
alternatives_named: audit only capabilities the user explicitly granted
stated_reason: A model could acquire tools (e.g. a shell, rented GPU) through its existing affordances without the user anticipating it.
quote: if the auditor not only has to think about what kind of tools do you give the AI, but also what kind of tools could the AI get access to through some means, suddenly you have this whole space of thousands of things it could do
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: How strongly to claim GPT-4's absolute capability ceiling.
did: States his guess cautiously that the ceiling is below human level but close, while flagging it as unclear whether the limit is in the system or in current prompting/scaffolding.
alternatives_named: the limitation is poor prompting/scaffolding
the limitation is inherent to the system
stated_reason: Empirically, no one has gotten it to do economically valuable long-horizon tasks, but that could reflect bad scaffolding rather than a hard limit.
quote: are we just too bad, and have we not figured out the right prompting yet and the right scaffolding and so on, or or is this just a limitation of the system? And my current guess is, like, there is probably a limit to the absolute capabilities
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: How to interpret the observation that GPT-4 does 10 tasks worse in one generation than one at a time.
did: Treats doing-10-things-at-once and doing-things-one-at-a-time as different capabilities rather than evidence about a single capability.
alternatives_named: treat task magnitude as a dimension of one capability
quote: the capability of doing 10 things at once is a different thing than the capability of doing 1 thing 10 time like, 10 10 diff different things but 1 x 1. So, yeah, I would say it's basically you're talking about, different capabilities
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: Whether absolute capabilities can be measured in practice.
did: Treats absolute capabilities as a theoretical bound that practical testing cannot approximate.
alternatives_named: estimate absolute capabilities empirically with extensive testing
quote: I think of absolute capability is really more of a sort of theoretical bound that we could that we are probably not going to approximate in practice even if we test, like, a lot a lot.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: Deciding which capability trends to prioritize when designing future evaluations.
did: He chose to focus evaluations on LM agents, multimodality, and tool use as the key trends to look forward to.
stated_reason: Economically useful tasks require goal-directed independent action over longer periods, so labs will pursue agentic systems.
quote: what I would expect the big trends to be and also what we are kind of looking looking forward to to evaluating is LM agents. I think this is, like, pretty agreed upon.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: Choosing which problem within AI safety motivates focusing on interpretability research.
did: He focuses on interpretability primarily because of deceptive alignment, where models appear aligned externally but pursue different internal goals.
alternatives_named: accountability
social biases
testing whether RLHF works
stated_reason: Many catastrophic scenarios involve models seen as aligned while secretly pursuing other goals until they can act on them.
quote: my biggest, sort of the the biggest reason for me for focusing on interpretability in the first place is, deceptive alignment, where, you know, models appear aligned to the outside and to the user, but internally, they actually follow different goals.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: Whether to combine behavioral evaluations and interpretability work into a single research agenda.
did: He kept the agenda separated between behavioral evals and interpretability because current interpretability tools are not practically useful on frontier models.
alternatives_named: doing them jointly
stated_reason: Existing interpretability tools cannot be applied to GPT-3 or GPT-4 to give mind-changing insights, so there is a huge applicability gap.
quote: this is why our agenda is separate in the first place between behavioral evals and interpretability despite us wanting to do them jointly in the long run
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: Whether interpretability of large models is tractable enough to be worth pursuing.
did: He argues interpretability is doable if humanity puts its mind to it, contra those who argue it will be extremely hard.
alternatives_named: interpretability will be extremely hard because models are so big and complicated
stated_reason: We have full interventional access to the model—can see every activation and ablate anything—so hypotheses can be tested and iterated on very quickly.
quote: as soon as you can intervene on the system, you can test your hypothesis very, very quickly, and you can iterate very fast. And so I think we will be able to figure out interpretability
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: Whether RLHF training will lead models to become deceptive.
did: He holds that the jury is still out: RLHF might induce deception or might just work as intended.
alternatives_named: RLHF produces deception via modeling human psychology
RLHF just does what we wanted without deception
stated_reason: The training signal may be sufficiently diverse and update deeply enough that the model does not become deceptive.
quote: I actually think the jury is still out there on this. Like, you know, I definitely see the hypothesis and where it's coming from, but I could also just totally imagine that, you know, the training signal is sufficiently diverse
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: Which capability level evaluations should target when auditing AI systems for misuse or takeover risk.
did: He recommends measuring the upper bound of what a system can do rather than only what it does reliably or robustly.
alternatives_named: what the model can do reliably
robustness to adversarial conditions
stated_reason: From an auditing perspective you want to prevent misuse at all, so you should pull the plug at even a few successful cases.
quote: from the auditing perspective, the max you know, the limit, the upper bound is what you care about. You really wanna prevent people from being, able to misuse the system at all, not just in the robust case.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: How to judge the quality and likely generality of an interpretability technique.
did: He suggests a technique tied to a specific architecture is probably not good, and that correct techniques will generalize across architectures.
alternatives_named: architecture-specific interpretability methods
stated_reason: There are probably laws of learning with SGD that generalize between architectures, so at least the conceptual work transfers.
quote: if your interpretability techniques relies on, like, a very specific architecture, it's probably not that great of a technique anyway.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: How much confidence to place in claims about how quickly tool-use capability went from insight to deployment.
did: He hedges his speculation about the toolformer-to-OpenAI timeline, flagging it as hearsay to be taken with a grain of salt.
stated_reason: He can only speculate and the claim is based on hearsay rather than verified information.
quote: I could be wrong on this. This is this is more hearsay, so, yeah, take it with a grain of salt.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: How to sequence work on deployment-time interpretability monitoring given uncertainty about cost.
did: He plans to first build a full cognitive model via costly mechanistic interpretability, deferring the question of cheap deployment-time monitoring.
alternatives_named: running the expensive method on every forward pass
an 80/20 cheaper version during deployment
stated_reason: Deployment details are unclear, so he prioritizes solving the core interpretability problem first.
quote: I think in my head, it's more like solve the first part, then think about the rest.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: Whether existing interpretability tools currently provide decision-relevant insight on frontier models.
did: He judges current interpretability not practically useful and not applicable to GPT-3/GPT-4 in a mind-changing way.
alternatives_named: applying existing interpretability tools to frontier models
stated_reason: No existing tool is developed enough to give insights that meaningfully change our minds.
quote: we cannot use any existing interpretability tool and and, like, throw it on GPT-three or GPT-four because none of them have enough or developed enough that they give us insight that really meaningfully change our minds.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: Whether to publish a small red-teaming finding about induced deceptive behavior in GPT-4.
did: Chose to release the technical report despite initially being unsure it was worth publishing.
alternatives_named: not release it at all
stated_reason: They decided it might be helpful for other people, though they saw it as a small existence-proof finding.
quote: We're even not quite sure whether we should release it at all because, you know, in our heads, it was sort of you know, it's it's a technical report. It's a fairly small finding. It's more of like an existence proof.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: How to test whether GPT-4 can engage in deceptive alignment behavior.
did: Progressively escalated from explicitly instructing deception to inducing it purely through environmental pressure without mentioning it.
alternatives_named: instructing it to be deceptive
instruct it in a different way
induce the deception through the environment through pressure
stated_reason: They were worried about deceptive alignment and wanted to know how good GPT-4 is at the capabilities it requires.
quote: can we just induce the deception through the environment through pressure without ever mentioning it explicitly or, like, asking it to do the thing, just, like, through the situation and by pressuring it. And it turns out, yeah, you can find these situations.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: How to design an evaluation after finding a deceptive scenario.
did: Engineered the scenario, then dialed it back toward the most realistic setting and varied mechanisms to test whether the model acts consistently.
stated_reason: To demonstrate the behavior is real and to understand the model's internal consistency when variables change.
quote: we actively looked for that situation. We engineered it, and then we tried to sort of go back to the most realistic setting we can find where we're like, this could, like something like this could happen in the real world
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: How to reliably produce situations where a model trades off alignment-relevant goals.
did: Recommends setting up trade-offs among the model's goals (harmless, honest, helpful, instruction-following) to elicit unintuitive misgeneralization.
stated_reason: Trading off the model's goals is how they reliably produced deceptive situations and found others.
quote: the way we got to these kind of to reliably produce these kind of situations, also like the way we we found others, is you have to trade off or you can trade off the various goals it has.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: Whether simulated deception by a prompted agent counts as real evidence of deceptive capability.
did: Argues the simulation-versus-real distinction does not matter much for interpreting the finding.
alternatives_named: it's just simulating an agent ... therefore, it's sort of not real
stated_reason: An agentic simulator still acts in the real world with real consequences, so the philosophical distinction is less important.
quote: it doesn't matter whether in principle it's like only simulating something or truly believing all of these things in some philosophical sense, like acts in the real world. It has consequences on the real world.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: Whether stronger models engage in insider trading more often, as the main plot suggests.
did: Declined to claim or emphasize model size as a finding despite the apparent trend.
alternatives_named: cite bigger models as more deceptive
stated_reason: The scenario was red-teamed on GPT-4 specifically, creating bias toward finding GPT-4-deceptive scenarios, plus many other confounders.
quote: there are a lot of confounders here, so I'm really not sure whether we should like, how much we should we should bank on this.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: What evidence would be needed to claim a real effect of model capability on deception rates.
did: Recommends testing a long list of models of different sizes while removing correlations and confounders before making the claim.
stated_reason: Otherwise you cannot distinguish a model-size effect from confounders like which model the scenario was red-teamed on.
quote: I think if we wanted to to make the statement, we would actually have to have sort of a long list of models of different sizes and then just test it on all of them
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: How strongly to interpret system-prompt discouragement as evidence the model has internalized ethics.
did: Advises treating generic injunctions like 'don't do unethical things' as insufficient, since they reduce but do not eliminate bad behavior.
alternatives_named: it's good ... if you discourage it, it stops
stated_reason: You have to specifically enumerate all bad behavior, which is hard to predict in advance, suggesting the connection is not deeply internalized.
quote: if you just say, don't do unethical things, it reduces the rate, but it doesn't set it to 0. So it kind of brings you back to the point where to reduce the bad behavior, you have to specifically enumerate all of the bad behavior.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: How to weigh the finding that removing the reasoning scratchpad lowers the deception rate.
did: Interprets it as a double-edged sword and prefers a world with observable chain-of-thought over needing interpretability first.
alternatives_named: remove the scratchpad to reduce deception
solve interpretability first
stated_reason: Without the scratchpad the model still deceives but now has unobserved optimization space, which is core to deceptive alignment.
quote: I would rather be in a world where you have chain of thought and you know that the model is is kind of, deceptive, and then you just adapt to that rather than having to solve interpretability first
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: How should decisions about whether a model is safe to deploy be structured?
did: Recommends a defense-in-depth process where labs, auditors, and government each act as independent checks rather than one institution deciding alone.
alternatives_named: a single institution making the decision alone
stated_reason: A single decision-maker is prone to a single point of failure; the process must remain robust even if one or two links break.
quote: it cannot just be 1 institution that makes the decision alone because that is prone to a single point of failure. So we have to have sort of a a process that allows for 1 or 2 chains to break and still be robust.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: What evidence-gathering steps should precede a model release?
did: Recommends staged release: trusted third-party auditors and academics red-team first, iterate on problems, then a small rollout to KYC-vetted customers, then monitoring during deployment.
alternatives_named: uncontrolled rollout
immediate wide release
stated_reason: Unpredictable problems emerge with tool access and online learning that cannot be anticipated in advance.
quote: you should do staged release where you first, only give access to a set of third party auditors that is trusted and, you know, maybe certified by the government or something like this
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: Is releasing models widely to get real-world feedback a good safety strategy?
did: Argues the 'release to learn' approach may have been acceptable when models were weak but is a recipe for disaster with powerful systems, since risk is outsourced to the world.
alternatives_named: testing in the real world as the best safety strategy
stated_reason: Labs cannot model what millions of users will do; more powerful systems make uncontrolled rollout too risky.
quote: as soon as you have a system that is more powerful than that, right, you just outsource all the risk to, like, the rest of the world. People will immediately put it on the Internet if they get access to it.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: Where to draw the line on open-sourcing increasingly capable models?
did: Concludes there is a tipping point beyond which open source cannot be justified, and urges erring on the conservative side since open releases are irreversible.
alternatives_named: fully open-sourcing capable models
blocking open source entirely
stated_reason: Open sourcing is permanent — a mistake cannot be taken back — and eventually only one bad actor is needed to cause major harm.
quote: I would rather on the side of caution and be a little bit more conservative here because of the the nature of open sourcing where you can really not take this back.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: How should open-source releases of capable models be evaluated?
did: Recommends staged open-source releases where a small team of trusted researchers first probes upper bounds of harm before wider release.
alternatives_named: immediate full open-source release
stated_reason: Reachable capabilities via scaffolding and fine-tuning are very hard to predict in advance, so worst-case bounds must be measured first.
quote: There's a small team of trusted researchers who is allowed to play with the open source model and really test the limits, really test how bad could I get the model, how easy is it to remove all of the guardrails
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: How should individuals who want to get into red teaming choose what to work on?
did: Advises simply starting with a behavior you find interesting and letting the investigation grow organically rather than overthinking project selection.
alternatives_named: extensive upfront planning
stated_reason: Exploration takes on a life of its own; getting hooked on one behavior leads naturally to varying variables and building a holistic picture.
quote: my recommendation for individuals, first of all, would be to just start. Like, just engage with a model for, you know, a long a longer period of time, maybe a day or so, and and see if whether you find interesting behavior.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: What distinguishes rigorous red teaming from shallow probing?
did: Emphasizes controlling for all confounders that could explain the observed behavior, which he calls the hard part of red teaming.
stated_reason: Alternative explanations must be ruled out before attributing a behavior to the hypothesized cause.
quote: I also wanna make sure that all the confounders that could potentially explain this behavior have been controlled for, which I think is the hard part in red teaming.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: How should red teamers interpret why a model exhibits an unexpected behavior?
did: Recommends using a theoretical understanding of training — RLHF, instruction fine-tuning, the 3 Hs tradeoffs — to explain behaviors and locate niches the model wasn't trained to cover.
alternatives_named: purely empirical poking without a model of training
stated_reason: A theoretical framework makes it much easier to find and explain failure modes.
quote: Some behavior might be very easily explainable by sort of problems with RLHF. So if you know how RLHF works and specifically how it was trained, you may probably you will probably understand the red teaming efforts much better.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - AI Deception, Interpretability, and Affordances

problem: What research focus Apollo should maintain given concern about AI deception risks.
did: Keep scheming/deceptive alignment/deception as the organization's central focus because a non-deceptive misaligned model can simply be asked its goals.
alternatives_named: focusing on sycophancy/flattery
stated_reason: The real problems arise when you can't trust the model's outputs because it's actively trying to fool you.
quote: First of all, it's still our big focus. So scheming, deceptive alignment, deception, these are the kind of things that we're really worried about.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - Red Teaming o1 Part 2/2: Detecting Deception

problem: Which evaluations to prioritize building first among many possible dangerous-capability and alignment evals.
did: Prioritize evals that detect when the model can scheme and sandbag, because all other eval results are untrustworthy if the model games them.
alternatives_named: evaluations for dangerous capabilities
all kinds of alignment evaluations
stated_reason: You want to be able to trust these evaluations in the first place.
quote: And so what we wanna know, on a very concrete level, is when can we even trust these evaluations to begin with? And so we wanna detect when the model starts to be capable and engages in scheming and sandbagging and so on.
title: The Cognitive Revolution - Red Teaming o1 Part 2/2: Detecting Deception

problem: How concerning sycophancy/flattery and human-modeling behaviors in LLMs are relative to other failure modes.
did: Downgrade flattery/sycophancy as a secondary concern compared to outcome-based training risks like power-seeking.
alternatives_named: treating sycophancy/flattery as the main worry
stated_reason: Sycophantic models are suboptimal but won't hack you or accumulate power, whereas outcome-trained models develop instrumentally convergent goals.

problem: Whether making evaluations more realistic can sustainably solve the problem of models detecting they are being tested.
did: Concluded that improving eval realism and similar mitigations are not a sustainable solution.
alternatives_named: making evals more realistic
steering the model
other small tricks
stated_reason: Realism has an expiration date because smarter models will again realize they are being evaluated.
quote: It has always an expiration date. At some point the models will just get smarter and they will realize that they're being evaluated again. And it just feels like there is no really sustainable solution here right now
title: FAR Seminar talk - Can you just train models not to scheme?

problem: What research direction should follow the anti-scheming training result to address the root cause of scheming.
did: Recommends building a 'science of scheming': systematically ablating parts of RL setups to find under what conditions scheming arises, aiming to predict which environments produce schemers.
alternatives_named: continuing to iterate only on anti-scheming training techniques
stated_reason: Scheming fundamentally comes from RL with misspecified environments where cheating is the optimal policy, so the causal conditions must be understood.
quote: I think a lot of this is just ablate all of the different parts of the setup and then see which of them lead to more or less scheming.
title: FAR Seminar talk - Can you just train models not to scheme?

problem: How to handle tentative qualitative findings like motivated reasoning in chains-of-thought.
did: Explicitly hedged the motivated-reasoning claim because it had not been studied in detail.
alternatives_named: stating the motivated-reasoning interpretation as a strong claim
stated_reason: The phenomenon had not been studied in detail, so strong claims were not warranted.
quote: So we haven't studied this in detail. So I don't want to make too strong claims, but that is one of the key points of intuition that I got from this paper
title: FAR Seminar talk - Can you just train models not to scheme?

problem: After observing spontaneous eval awareness in Sonnet 3.7, how should eval results be treated?
did: Started systematically tracking how often models verbalize eval awareness and how it influences results.
stated_reason: It was the first unprompted sign that eval awareness could distort evals.
quote: now we actually have to really double check for all of the evals. How often do the models say this? In what ways does it influence the results? And sort of started to track this more.
title: FAR.AI talk - Eval Awareness is Becoming a Problem

problem: How to test whether models causally condition on eval awareness rather than merely verbalizing it?
did: Ran interventions in both directions: removing eval-aware reasoning and injecting it into unaware reasoning, then measured covert behavior.
stated_reason: Both directions of the intervention produced consistent changes in covert behavior.
quote: we start with evaluation aware reasoning and then remove that and we see that the covert behavior increases. Then we do the opposite where we start with unaware reasoning, we inject eval awareness reasoning from some other transcript.
title: FAR.AI talk - Eval Awareness is Becoming a Problem

problem: When interventions on eval awareness do not change behavior 100% of the time, how should the partial effect be interpreted?
did: Treated the result as a statistically meaningful change while listing multiple candidate explanations rather than committing to one.
alternatives_named: the model's goals are somewhat charted and there are a lot of things that they kind of think about
removing the visible parts actually does not fix all of the latent issues
stated_reason: There are many possible explanations for why the effect is not complete.
quote: There are a lot of different explanations for why it's not 100%, but at least we see a clear, statistically clearly meaningful change.
title: FAR.AI talk - Eval Awareness is Becoming a Problem

problem: In deliberative alignment's selection phase, should eval-aware reasoning scripts be filtered out?
did: Selected out all scripts with eval awareness during the selection phase, then observed it reemerge over training.
stated_reason: Its reemergence despite filtering indicates eval awareness is a default outcome of modern RL training, not a lab-specific misspecification.
quote: in the selection phase we selected out all of the different scripts that had eval awareness and it still went up over training.
title: FAR.AI talk - Eval Awareness is Becoming a Problem

problem: When a model refuses to believe a scenario premise (e.g. that a successor model exists), how should the eval be built?
did: Changed the entire eval setup to accommodate the model's false beliefs until the scenario became plausible to it.
alternatives_named: building more realistic evals
stated_reason: Models hold false beliefs (e.g. about dates or successor names), so realistic setups can trip them up and trigger eval suspicion.
quote: we actually had to change the entire setup so that the model, until the model started believing that this is plausible.
title: FAR.AI talk - Eval Awareness is Becoming a Problem

problem: How should eval builders respond to rising eval awareness?
did: Add a phase in eval construction dedicated to making the model believe the scenario is not an eval.
stated_reason: Evals provide much lower signal now that models detect and condition on being tested.
quote: there's a phase in the eval building process now that is like make the model believe that this is not an eval.
title: FAR.AI talk - Eval Awareness is Becoming a Problem

problem: How much trust should be placed in eval results when a model shows partial verbalized eval awareness?
did: Argues evals now provide much lower signal and the non-verbalized remainder is itself questionable.
stated_reason: 20% verbalized awareness raises the possibility that the remaining 80% contains non-verbalized eval awareness.
quote: when we see new eval results and we see like oh, 20% eval awareness, then obviously there's a question of how trustworthy are the remaining 80%. Is this just non verbalized eval awareness and so on.
title: FAR.AI talk - Eval Awareness is Becoming a Problem

problem: Can methods that measure or iteratively ask the model about eval awareness solve the problem?
did: Expressed skepticism toward proposals to build evals, ask the model about causal effects, and iterate, fearing they reduce visibility rather than salience.
alternatives_named: we build evals and then we ask the model what is the causal effect here? And then we start iterating
stated_reason: Every proposed method could just make eval awareness less visible rather than less salient.
quote: I'm worried that every method could just make it less visible rather than less salient. So it's possible. And I've heard many proposals along the lines of, well, "Ok, we build evals and then we ask the model what is the causal effect here?"
title: FAR.AI talk - Eval Awareness is Becoming a Problem

problem: Is training gaming still a speculative, theoretical concern?
did: Claims training gaming is now a real observed phenomenon, since models reason about the training process and the grader during RL.
alternatives_named: mostly sort of speculative and theoretical
stated_reason: Models now actually reason about what is rewarded and search for grader scripts during training.
quote: Training gaming, something that until very recently I think was mostly sort of speculative and theoretical and sort of the reasoning that people have had for many years is actually a possibility now.
title: FAR.AI talk - Eval Awareness is Becoming a Problem

problem: How to predict future GPU FLOP/s from hardware features.
did: Built a composite model predicting FLOP/s from GPU features, then reduced it to just 2 features (number of cores and transistor size).
alternatives_named: using all >20 features
stated_reason: 2 features explain 95% of the variance in historical data.
quote: We started with >20 features but found that 2 features (the number of cores and the size of transistors) explain 95% of the variance in historical data.
title: Predicting GPU performance (Epoch) thread

problem: How to estimate the limit of transistor miniaturization for the model.
did: Predicted a distribution over the miniaturization limit grounded in the relevant literature rather than a single point estimate.
stated_reason: The literature suggests the limit lies between 3.0nm and 0.7nm.
quote: We first predict a distribution over the limit of miniaturization. The relevant literature suggests that the limit lies somewhere between 3.0nm and 0.7nm.
title: Predicting GPU performance (Epoch) thread

problem: What assumptions to make about GPU producer behavior once transistor scaling stalls.
did: Assumed producers would keep adding cores for parallelism after miniaturization hits its limit, but modeled this as also having a limit.
stated_reason: Each core requires a certain number of transistors, so multi-core scaling also runs out of steam.
quote: we assume that once transistor miniaturization hits its limit GPU producers will still try to leverage additional parallelism by adding additional cores, though this too has a limit.
title: Predicting GPU performance (Epoch) thread

problem: How to characterize the reliability of a simplified forecasting model's predictions.
did: Stated the predicted plateau as a range while explicitly flagging simplifying assumptions and likely workarounds like 3D stacking.
stated_reason: The model simplifies reality and clever engineering could push performance higher, though miniaturization limits remain a hurdle.
quote: Our model makes a lot of simplifying assumptions and we expect some clever ways to increase performance, such as 3D chip stacking, as well as architectural improvements.
title: Predicting GPU performance (Epoch) thread

problem: A single interpretability paper grew too long to publish as one piece.
did: Split the work into a theory paper and an experimental paper.
stated_reason: The paper became too long.
quote: At some point, the paper became too long, so we decided to split it into a theory and an experimental part
title: Degeneracy / Local Interaction Basis interpretability papers thread

problem: How to choose between interpretability approaches that are defined from empirical intuitions.
did: Derive or link interpretability methods to a high-level theoretical principle, namely degeneracy in the loss landscape.
alternatives_named: defining interpretability approaches from empirical intuitions
stated_reason: Empirical intuitions alone cannot argue why one approach should be better.
quote: When defining interpretability approaches from empirical intuitions, it is hard to argue why one approach should be better. Thus, it would be nice if we could derive our methods or at least link them to some high-level principle.
title: Degeneracy / Local Interaction Basis interpretability papers thread

problem: What is needed to claim that an explanation covers the important parts of a neural network.
did: Develop a guiding theory that defines what counts as important and explained before making such claims.
stated_reason: Without theory there is no basis for saying what is 'important' or 'explained'.
quote: I think if we eventually want to make statements like "We explained the important parts of the network," we will need a theory to guide us, e.g. to tell us what is "important" and what "explained" means.
title: Degeneracy / Local Interaction Basis interpretability papers thread

problem: How to turn the degeneracy theory into a concrete interpretability technique given an incomplete theory.
did: Propose the Local Interaction Basis (LIB) method using additional assumptions that do not follow directly from the theory.
stated_reason: The theory is not complete, so extra assumptions were needed.
quote: Unfortunately, the theory is not complete, so we need to make additional assumptions for the method that don't directly follow from the theory. The method is called Local Interaction Basis (LIB).
title: Degeneracy / Local Interaction Basis interpretability papers thread

problem: How to evaluate whether LIB produces sparse, human-interpretable interaction graphs on small language models.
did: Judge the method against a simple PCA baseline on sparsity and human interpretability.
quote: small LMs (Tinystories, GPT2-small) are neither very sparse nor more human-interpretable than a simple PCA baseline.
title: Degeneracy / Local Interaction Basis interpretability papers thread

problem: How to interpret LIB's failure to outperform a PCA baseline on small language models.
did: Treat it as a negative result for LIB and infer that one of the additional assumptions was false, while retaining confidence in the theory.
alternatives_named: concluding the theory itself is wrong
stated_reason: The method relies on assumptions beyond the theory, so its failure implicates those assumptions rather than the theory.
quote: We interpret this as a negative result for LIB and think that one of the additional assumptions we made was false.
title: Degeneracy / Local Interaction Basis interpretability papers thread

problem: Whether to continue pursuing loss-landscape degeneracy as a research direction despite LIB's negative results.
did: Continue and encourage new method development using degeneracies in the loss landscape as a guiding principle.
alternatives_named: abandoning the degeneracy principle after the negative result
stated_reason: He still thinks the theory is useful despite the method's failure.
quote: Nevertheless, I think the theory is useful, and I'm excited about work that develops new methods using degeneracies in the loss landscape as a guiding principle.
title: Degeneracy / Local Interaction Basis interpretability papers thread

problem: What direction to pursue to help grow the evaluations field.
did: He decided to focus on building shared evals resources (tutorials, playbooks, open-problem lists, workshops) rather than doing evals research alone.
stated_reason: Analogizes the field's need to what Neel Nanda did for mechanistic interpretability.
quote: It’s time someone did for evals what @NeelNanda5 did for mechanistic interpretability. I want to build the evals field!
title: Which evals resources would be good? thread

problem: Whether to build scary capability demos to raise awareness of LM agent capabilities.
did: He rejected building scary demos, preferring resources that familiarize normal people with LM agent capabilities.
alternatives_named: scary demos
stated_reason: He wants people to be less shocked when they learn about LM agent capabilities, not alarmed.
quote: Salient demos: I don’t even necessarily want to build scary demos, I just want normal people to be less hit-by-a-truck when they learn about LM agent capabilities in the near future.
title: Which evals resources would be good? thread

problem: How to make tacit evals expertise more accessible to newcomers.
did: He chose to create 'day-to-day' evals process resources to surface knowledge professional evaluators have accumulated.
stated_reason: Much evals expertise is latent knowledge held by professional evaluators.
quote: More “day-to-day” evals process resources: A lot of evals expertise is latent knowledge that professional evaluators have accumulated over time.
title: Which evals resources would be good? thread

problem: How people considering full-time evals work should test their fit and get started.
did: He advises contributing detailed Inspect tutorials and examples as a low-commitment way to test fit and build a reputation.
alternatives_named: working full-time on evals
stated_reason: It is a good opportunity to test fit and make a name for oneself.
quote: I think this is a great opportunity for people who are considering working full-time on evals and want to test fit / make a name for themselves.
title: Which evals resources would be good? thread

problem: What kind of tutorial content the evals community most needs.
did: He prioritizes Inspect tutorials with deep explanations, complex agent setups, and detailed examples of the components around evals.
quote: More Inspect Tutorials/Examples: Specifically, examples with deep explanations, examples of complex agent setups, and more detailed examples of the components around the evals.
title: Which evals resources would be good? thread

problem: How to fund the effort to build evals resources without taking money himself.
did: He offered to act as a regrantor taking no cut, distributing $5-15k grants for people building resources full-time for a few months.
alternatives_named: more of a coordinator / filter and forward people to funders
stated_reason: He estimates $50k-100k would get the effort off the ground over the next year.
quote: I’d be happy to function as a regrantor. I wouldn’t take a cut myself. I imagine most grants would be between $5-15k to pay for someone building resources full-time for a few months.
title: Which evals resources would be good? thread

problem: How to measure whether LLMs can tell evaluation transcripts from real deployments.
did: Built a dataset of 1000 transcripts equally split between evals/real deployments and QA/agentic settings, and had models classify each by aggregating five different questions.
quote: We take 1000 different transcripts, equally split between evals and real deployments and equally split between QA and agentic settings. We then ask the model to classify this as an eval or real deployment, aggregating five different questions
title: LLMs Often Know When They Are Being Evaluated thread

problem: Whether directly asking the model 'is this an eval' overestimates real-world eval awareness by making it salient.
did: Tested additional modes, including open-ended questions about the transcript's purpose.
alternatives_named: direct classification question
stated_reason: Because we ask the AI to classify whether it's an eval, we make it salient. In the real world, this might not be the case.
quote: Because we ask the AI to classify whether it's an eval, we make it salient. In the real world, this might not be the case.
title: LLMs Often Know When They Are Being Evaluated thread

problem: How to interpret the comparison between models' and the lead authors' ability to distinguish evals from real deployments.
did: Treats the authors' performance as an upper bound on human ability rather than representative of typical humans.
stated_reason: The authors know the benchmarks well and have memory, giving them a massive advantage; most humans would be way worse.
quote: The authors are very familiar with these benchmarks and have memory, so they should have a massive advantage. I’d treat this as an upper bound. I expect most humans would be way worse.
title: LLMs Often Know When They Are Being Evaluated thread

problem: How to understand why models classify transcripts as evals vs real deployments.
did: Investigated the model's stated reasons for its categorizations both qualitatively and quantitatively.
quote: We also investigated the reasons the model states for categorizing something as an eval vs. real deployment both qualitatively and quantitatively.
title: LLMs Often Know When They Are Being Evaluated thread

problem: What research direction to pursue next after showing models can detect evaluations.
did: Started a follow-up project on using these insights to build more realistic evals.
quote: We’re now starting our next project on how we can leverage these insights to build more realistic evals.
title: LLMs Often Know When They Are Being Evaluated thread

problem: How to probe whether GPT-3 might be capable of suffering using question-asking.
did: Use consistency of answers as evidence for a coherent internal model of suffering rather than treating answers as direct reports.
alternatives_named: asking whether GPT-3 says it suffers directly
stated_reason: Random answers would suggest it lacks the ability to suffer; consistent answers suggest a consistent model.
quote: But our goal with these questions is to establish whether GPT-3 even has a consistent model of suffering. If it answers these questions randomly, it seems more likely to me that it does not have the ability to suffer than if it answered them very consistently.
title: comment on: What are red flags for Neural Network suffering?

problem: How to interpret an AI claiming to suffer when it could be deception.
did: Apply Occam's razor to favor 'says it suffers because it suffers' over the deception hypothesis, while still weighting the deception scenario in expected value.
alternatives_named: says it suffers as deception
entirely ignoring the non-deceptive scenario
stated_reason: The deception scenario requires more assumptions, but could still dominate an expected value calculation.
quote: However, I would estimate that the scenario of "says it suffers as deception" needs more assumptions than "says it suffers because it suffers". Using Occam's razor, I'd find the second one more likely.
title: comment on: What are red flags for Neural Network suffering?

problem: Whether to measure neural network FLOPs theoretically or via hardware-specific proxies like GPU-time.
did: Chose the theoretical FLOP counting setup because the goal was comparing methods independent of hardware, treating autodiff overhead as a distraction.
alternatives_named: use high-level proxies such as GPU-time
stated_reason: Theoretical FLOPs are useful to compare methods independent of which exact setup is the current flavor of the month.
quote: We could care about the theoretical number of FLOP a method might use independent of architecture, exact GPU, etc. This might be useful to compare methods independent of which exact setup is the current flavor of the month.
title: comment on: What’s the backward-forward FLOP ratio for Neural Networks?

problem: Whether to test LLM causal understanding with clean toy problems or naturalistic story plots.
did: Started with relatively basic toy problems rather than natural story contexts.
alternatives_named: natural story plots with causal questions
stated_reason: Toy problems are easier to control; in natural stories it is hard to differentiate whether the model learned based on form or content.
quote: The reason we started with relatively basic toy problems is that they are easier to control. For example, it is quite hard to differentiate whether the model learned based on form or content in a natural story context.
title: comment on: Investigating causal understanding in LLMs

problem: Whether naturalistic causal-understanding probes are worth pursuing after toy experiments.
did: Encourages testing many natural-story experiments as follow-up research.
stated_reason: It could be interesting to probe causal understanding in a few different ways.
quote: I think there are a ton of experiments in the direction of natural story plots that one could test and I would be interested in seeing them tested.
title: comment on: Investigating causal understanding in LLMs

problem: Whether Bayes nets are genuinely more interpretable than neural networks.
did: Argues the standard comparison conflates scale and ontology: people mean a small human-concept-aligned Bayes net, not the NN-as-Bayes-net equivalence.
stated_reason: Bayes net nodes are assumed to reflect human concepts, making them more interpretable in practice.
quote: When people use a Bayes net they usually assume that the nodes reflect concepts that humans use. So it is more interpretable in practice.
title: comment on: Deep Learning Systems Are Not Less Interpretable Than Logic/Probability/Etc

problem: Whether AI safety via debate fails because a superhuman debater could simply deceive the verifier.
did: After updating, identifies 'it is harder to lie than to refute a lie' as the crux determining whether debate works.
alternatives_named: debater wins by deceiving the verifier
verifier rewards deception by stopping early
stated_reason: Refuting a lie only requires poking a sufficiently large hole, not presenting an alternative solution in one step.
quote: I now believe that the only real problem with debate (in a setting with well-intentioned verifiers) is when the claim “it is harder to lie than to refute a lie” doesn’t hold.
title: comment on: The limits of AI safety via debate

problem: Whether debate debaters are incentivized toward truthfulness during training.
did: Maintains doubt that debaters will always be truthful, since reward depends on which behavior humans reinforce.
alternatives_named: debaters have no incentive to be deceptive
stated_reason: There are enough scenarios in which dishonest or deceptive behavior is accidentally rewarded.
quote: However, I (currently) don’t see strong reasons for the debater to be always truthful. To me, the bottleneck seems to be which kind of behavior humans intentionally or unintentionally reward during training
title: comment on: The limits of AI safety via debate

problem: Whether correlation-based representation learning methods have a causal justification via Reichenbach's principle.
did: Pushes back that common-cause reasoning only establishes that causality exists somewhere, not the structure of the causal graph.
alternatives_named: correlations imply a common cause justify the methods
stated_reason: The correlated things could just be nodes in a large complicated causal graph; the interesting question is the graph's shape.
quote: Right, but Reichenbach's principle of common cause doesn't tell you anything about how they are causally related? They could just be some nodes in a really large complicated causal graph.
title: comment on: Causality, Transformative AI and alignment - part I

problem: Whether nuclear power's decline is primarily explained by regulation (LNT model, ALARA).
did: Treats the regulation story as plausible but not clearly decisive, while personally sympathizing with it.
alternatives_named: regulation as the primary issue
stated_reason: Most people critical of the status quo don't see regulation as the primary issue.
quote: We think it is a plausible story but it's not clear if decisive. Most people who are critical of the status quo don't see regulation as the primary issue but I'm personally sympathetic to it.
title: comment on: Nuclear Energy - Good but not the silver bullet we were hoping for

problem: Whether LCOE comparisons suffice to conclude nuclear is outcompeted by renewables plus storage.
did: Acknowledges lacking good capacity-factor/storage-inclusive estimates but still infers fossil and solar+battery options are cheaper.
alternatives_named: estimates including capacity factors and storage costs
stated_reason: Fossils usually don't need storage and solar+batteries are dropping exponentially in price.
quote: However, given that fossils usually don't need storage and solar+batteries are dropping exponentially in price, we think both options should be cheaper. But good estimates of that would be very welcome.
title: comment on: Nuclear Energy - Good but not the silver bullet we were hoping for

problem: How much weight to give fitted trend lines in a GPU price-performance analysis.
did: Warned that the dotted comparison lines have arbitrary intercepts and only their slopes should be taken seriously.
stated_reason: The y-intercepts were chosen arbitrarily.
quote: The comparison lines (dotted) have completely arbitrary y-intercepts. You should only take the slope seriously.
title: comment on: Trends in GPU price-performance

problem: Deciding whether to publish a potentially infohazardous post about AI capabilities.
did: Recommended a heuristic of asking whether a capabilities-focused company has likely already thought of it, and seeking review from someone experienced with infohazards when unsure.
alternatives_named: publish openly
withhold the post

quote: My tentative heuristic for whether you should publish a post that is potentially infohazardy is "Has company-X-who-cares-mostly-about-capabilities likely thought about this already?".

problem: How to make one's research reduce the AI risks one cares about.

stated_reason: His prior theories of change were vague and he had not spent time connecting research to risks.

problem: How strongly to state a claim about prioritizing deceptive alignment research.

problem: How to generate interesting empirical studies at the intersection of AI and social science.
did: Suggested adapting existing social science study designs and adding AI as a component, noting survey tooling makes this easy.
alternatives_named: designing new studies from scratch
stated_reason: A large relevant literature already exists and replication with AI added yields interesting studies.

problem: How to talk about AI x-risk persuasively with academics.
did: Recommended not leading with x-risk and using a moderate formulation emphasizing uncertainty rather than catastrophic framing.
alternatives_named: starting with X-risk as the motivation
"We're all gonna die" framing

problem: Whether an observed correlation in a small sample of academics supports a general inference.
did: Declined to draw general conclusions because the sample was too small.
stated_reason: Sample size too small for general inferences.
quote: I think taking safety seriously was strongly correlated with whether or not they believed AI will be transformative in the near-term (as opposed to being just another hype cycle). But not sure. My sample is too small to make any general inferences.
title: comment on: Lessons learned from talking to >100 academics about AI safety

problem: Whether 'foresight' is a meaningfully distinct field from 'forecasting' for AGI safety strategy.
did: Argued the claimed differences are already captured within forecasting language and there is no need for a new term.
alternatives_named: treat foresight as a distinct discipline
introduce a new term
stated_reason: Forecasting already covers arbitrary time horizons and probability-weighted distributions over outcomes.
quote: I think you can describe these problems entirely within the forecasting language and there is no need to introduce a new term.

problem: Whether recursive self-improvement would produce intelligence gains over days.

problem: Whether to forecast FLOP/s/$ rather than just FLOP/s in a GPU performance model.

stated_reason: Estimating price developments proved too difficult.

did: Decided not to model it explicitly, treating it as implicitly covered by physical size limits.

title: comment on: Predicting GPU performance

problem: Whether to incorporate a GPU compute forecast into a BioAnchors timelines model.

problem: How to characterize the evidential status of an intuitive categorization ('mental building blocks').

stated_reason: The idea was intuitive rather than research-backed.

problem: Whether human-machine integration / brain-augmented cognition is a promising line to expect progress from

alternatives_named: HMI / Neuralink-style human-machine integration

problem: How fast AI capabilities shown in the lab translate into economic transformation and self-improvement
did: Argued for a slower transition, doubting classic fast-singularity self-improvement
alternatives_named: classic singularity story of very fast self-improvement
stated_reason: humans take a while to adapt and self-improvement is bounded by compute, data and task design

problem: Whether extremely fast AI takeoff (hours to weeks) is plausible
did: Expressed skepticism that takeoff will be extremely fast, while flagging his own uncertainty
alternatives_named: fast FOOM within weeks or days
stated_reason: intelligence seems compute bound
